title: From cron jobs to a job queue
description: A 15-minute team talk in four parts; open a part for its slides and speaker notes

blocks.title: The problem
blocks.description: Cron jobs fail without a sound

children.title: 40 jobs, one crontab
children.description: Exports, emails and cleanups on a single server
children.details: Everything that runs on a schedule lives in one crontab on one machine. Nobody owns it as a whole; each team added its lines over five years.

children.title: Failures nobody saw
children.description: A broken export was found by a customer, nine days late
children.details: A cron job that fails writes to a log nobody reads. The nightly export to our biggest customer failed for nine days before they asked where their files were.

children.title: Overlapping runs
children.description: A slow run overlapped the next one and locked tables
children.details: When the invoice job took longer than an hour, the next run started anyway. Two runs locked the same rows and checkout stalled at 2 a.m.

blocks.title: Three options
blocks.description: Each one tried for a weekend

children.title: A hosted queue
children.description: Reliable and managed, but one more service and one more bill
children.details: Works well, but every job now needs network access and credentials for a new service, and local development needs an emulator.

children.title: Redis and a worker
children.description: Fast and popular, but Redis would hold state we must not lose
children.details: Our Redis is a cache: we restart it freely and do not back it up. Keeping jobs there would turn a cache into a database.

children.title: A queue in Postgres
children.description: Jobs as rows in the database we already run and back up
children.details: Workers take the next job with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. No new service; a job and the data it changes commit in one transaction.

blocks.title: The choice
blocks.description: A queue in our own database

children.title: How it works
children.description: A jobs table, a scheduler that adds rows, workers that take them
children.details:
```sql
SELECT * FROM jobs
WHERE run_at <= now() AND state = 'ready'
ORDER BY run_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```

The scheduler only inserts rows; any number of workers can take them.

children.title: Retries and dead jobs
children.description: Three tries with back-off, then an alert with the error
children.details: A failed job is retried after 1, 5 and 30 minutes. After the third failure it is marked dead, and the on-call channel gets the job name and the error.

children.title: Moving job by job
children.description: One job a day, the noisiest first; cron kept as a fallback
children.details: Each job moved on its own day, with its cron line commented out, not deleted, for two weeks. Nothing had to be rolled back.

children.title: Failures in minutes
children.description: Every failed job reaches the on-call channel
children.details: The median time from a failure to someone looking at it went from days (when a customer noticed) to under ten minutes.

children.title: Quieter nights
children.description: No more overlapping runs: one worker per job at a time
children.details: Overlaps are impossible by design: a running job holds its row. Night pages about locked tables stopped.

children.title: What we would do again
children.description: Start with the noisiest job, keep the old path for a while
children.details: Moving one job a day kept every change small enough to explain in a sentence. The table of jobs became the documentation nobody wrote before.
